title: Types of Variables and Commonly Used Statistical Designs -- Definition/Introduction
content: An appropriate statistical design is a critical factor in drawing inferences from any research or scientific study. [1] Numerous statistical designs are now feasible due to advances in data analysis software. [1] Healthcare providers must possess some statistical knowledge to interpret new studies and provide up-to-date patient care. We present an overview of variable types and common design patterns to facilitate understanding. [2]

title: Types of Variables and Commonly Used Statistical Designs -- Issues of Concern
content: Individuals who attempt to conduct research and choose an inappropriate design may select a flawed test and draw erroneous conclusions. This decision could lead to work being rejected for publication or (worse) lead to erroneous clinical decision-making, resulting in unsafe practice. [1] By understanding variable types and selecting tests appropriate to the data, individuals can draw sound conclusions and support their work for an application. [3]

title: Types of Variables and Commonly Used Statistical Designs -- Issues of Concern -- Variables
content: To determine which statistical design is appropriate for the data and research plan, one must first examine the scales of each measurement. [4] Multiple variable types determine the appropriate design.

title: Types of Variables and Commonly Used Statistical Designs -- Issues of Concern -- Variables
content: Ordinal data (also sometimes referred to as discrete) provide ranks and thus degrees of difference between measurements. [5] Likert items can serve as ordinal variables, but the Likert scale, the result of adding all the times, can be treated as a continuous variable. [6] For example, on a 20-item scale with each item ranging from 1 to 5, the item itself can be an ordinal variable, whereas if you add up all items, it could result in a range from 20 to 100. A general guideline for determining if a variable is ordinal vs continuous: if the variable has more than 10 options, it can be treated as a continuous variable. [7] The following examples are ordinal variables: Likert items Cancer stages Residency Year

title: Types of Variables and Commonly Used Statistical Designs -- Issues of Concern -- Nominal, Categorical, Dichotomous, Binary
content: Other variable types use interchangeable terms. Nominal and categorical variables describe samples in groups based on counts that fall within each category, have no quantitative relationships, and cannot be ranked. [8] Examples of these variables include: Service (ie, emergency, internal medicine, and psychiatry) Ethnicity Mode of Arrival (ambulance, helicopter, car)

title: Types of Variables and Commonly Used Statistical Designs -- Issues of Concern -- Nominal, Categorical, Dichotomous, Binary
content: A dichotomous or a binary variable is in the same family as nominal/categorical, but this type has only 2 options. Binary logistic regression, discussed below, has 2 options for the outcome of interest in the analysis. Often used as (yes/no), examples of dichotomous or binary variables would be: Alive (yes vs no) Insurance (yes vs no) Readmitted (yes vs no)

title: Types of Variables and Commonly Used Statistical Designs -- Issues of Concern -- Nominal, Categorical, Dichotomous, Binary
content: With this overview of variable types, commonly used statistical designs for different measurement scales are presented. Importantly, before selecting a statistical test, individuals should perform exploratory data analysis to ensure data integrity and consider type I and type II errors, as well as power. Furthermore, investigators should ensure that appropriate statistical assumptions are met. [9] [10] For example, parametric tests, including those discussed below (t-tests, analysis of variance (ANOVA), correlation, and regression), require that the data follow a normal distribution and that the variances within each group be similar. [6] [11] After addressing issues identified through exploratory data analysis and reducing the risk of type I and type II errors, a statistical test can be selected. Below is a brief introduction to the most commonly used statistical designs, with examples of each. An example of 1 research focus, with each statistical design type discussed, is provided in Table 1 to illustrate commonly used designs.

title: Types of Variables and Commonly Used Statistical Designs -- Issues of Concern -- Independent Samples T-test
content: An independent samples t-test allows a comparison of 2 groups of subjects on 1 (continuous) variable. Examples in biomedical research include comparing treatment outcomes with control-group results and examining differences in males vs females. Example: Does adherence to the ketogenic diet (yes/no; 2 groups) have a differential effect on total sleep time (minutes; continuous)?

title: Types of Variables and Commonly Used Statistical Designs -- Issues of Concern -- Paired T-test
content: A paired t-test analyzes a single sample, measuring the same variable on 2 occasions; this is often useful in intervention and educational research. Example : Does participating in a research curriculum (one group with intervention) improve resident performance on a test to measure research competence (continuous)?

title: Types of Variables and Commonly Used Statistical Designs -- Issues of Concern -- One-Way Analysis of Variance (ANOVA)
content: Analysis of variance (ANOVA), an extension of the t-test, tests differences among more than 2 groups (independent variables) using a dependent variable. [11] ANOVA is preferable to conducting multiple t-tests as it reduces the likelihood of committing a Type I error. Example: Are there differences in length of stay in the hospital (continuous) based on the mode of arrival (car, ambulance, helicopter, 3 groups)?

title: Types of Variables and Commonly Used Statistical Designs -- Issues of Concern -- Repeated Measures ANOVA
content: Another procedure commonly used when data for individuals are repeated (repeatedly measured) is repeated-measures ANOVA. [1] In these studies, multiple measurements of the dependent variable are collected from the study participants. [11] A within-subjects repeated measures ANOVA determines effects based on the treatment variable alone, whereas mixed ANOVAs allow both between-group effects and within-subjects to be considered. Within-Subjects Example: How does ketamine affect mean arterial pressure (continuous variable) over time (repeated measurement)?

title: Types of Variables and Commonly Used Statistical Designs -- Issues of Concern -- Nonparametric Tests
content: Nonparametric tests, such as the Mann-Whitney U test (2 groups; nonparametric t-test), Kruskal Wallis test (multiple groups; nonparametric ANOVA), Spearman’s rho (nonparametric correlation coefficient) can be used when data are ordinal or lack normality. [3] [5] Not requiring normality means these tests can analyze skewed data; they require fewer assumptions. [11]

title: Types of Variables and Commonly Used Statistical Designs -- Issues of Concern -- Chi-square
content: A Chi-square test determines the effect of relationships between categorical variables, which determines frequencies and proportions into which these variables fall. [11] As with other tests discussed, variants and extensions of the chi-square test (eg, Fisher’s exact test, the McNemar test) may be suitable depending on the variables. [8] Example: Is there a relationship between individuals with methamphetamine in their system (yes vs no; dichotomous) and gender (male or female; dichotomous)?

title: Types of Variables and Commonly Used Statistical Designs -- Issues of Concern -- Correlation
content: Correlations (used interchangeably with ‘associations’) signal patterns in data between variables. [1] A positive association occurs if values in 1 variable increase as values in another also increase. A negative association occurs when 1 variable decreases as the other increases. A correlation coefficient, expressed as r, describes the strength of the relationship: a value of 0 means no relationship, and the relationship strengthens as r approaches 1 (positive relationship) or -1 (negative association). [5] Example: Is there a relationship between age (continuous) and satisfaction with life survey scores (continuous)?

title: Types of Variables and Commonly Used Statistical Designs -- Issues of Concern -- Linear Regression
content: Regression allows researchers to quantify the strength of relationships between a dependent variable and independent variables and yields a predictive equation. [11] A large number of variables are usable in regression methods. Example: Which admission to the hospital metrics (multiple continuous) best predict the total length of stay (minutes; continuous)?

title: Types of Variables and Commonly Used Statistical Designs -- Issues of Concern -- Binary Logistic Regression
content: This type of regression, which aims to predict an outcome, is appropriate when the dependent variable is binary (yes/no; cured/not cured). [12] Example: Which panel results (multiple of continuous, ordinal, categorical, dichotomous) best predict whether or not an individual has a positive blood culture (dichotomous/binary)?

title: Types of Variables and Commonly Used Statistical Designs -- Clinical Significance
content: Although numerous other statistical designs and extensions of the methods covered in this topic exist, the above information provides a starting point for healthcare providers to become familiar with variables and commonly used designs. Researchers should examine variable types before selecting statistical tests to obtain relevant measures and valid study results. [6] There is a recommendation to consult a statistician to ensure appropriate use of the statistical design, given the variables, and that the assumptions are met. [1] With the variety of statistical software available, investigators must a priori understand the type of statistical tests when designing a study. [13] All providers must interpret and critically appraise journal publications to make evidence-based clinical decisions, and this is enhanced by a limited yet sound understanding of variables and commonly used study designs. [14]

title: Types of Variables and Commonly Used Statistical Designs -- Nursing, Allied Health, and Interprofessional Team Interventions
content: All interprofessional healthcare team members need to be familiar with study design and the variables used in studies to accurately evaluate new data and studies as they are published, and apply the latest data to patient care and drive optimal outcomes.
